title: Limits on the atomic description of four-wave mixing
authors: Irvin F. Ángeles-Aguillón, Nieves Arias-Téllez, Pablo Yanes-Thomas, Alejandro Kunold, Daniel Sahagún-Sánchez
abstract: The limits of the well-established single-atom model for describing photon-pair generation via four-wave mixing in a diamond configuration in atomic ensembles are experimentally tested. Using a cold-atom source, biphotons are generated and detected through polarization analyzers that resolve the emitted light into horizontal and vertical components in the laboratory frame. The pump lasers driving the first and second excitation transitions are horizontally and vertically polarized, respectively. To predict single-photon counts and coincidence rates in all polarization channels, the first- and second-order correlation functions are calculated directly using a comprehensive model that accounts for all Zeeman sublevels of the relevant hyperfine states. Furthermore, the population dynamics with and without the re-pump laser of the magneto-optical trap are compared, revealing substantial differences in the populations of the Zeeman sublevels. This motivates the inclusion of two additional hyperfine levels and their corresponding Zeeman sublevels in the final model. The resulting density matrix is used to calculate expectation values of the far-field electric-field operators and compare them with experimental measurements over a range of pump-laser powers. Excellent agreement with the measured photon counts is obtained over most of this range. For the coincidence measurements, good agreement is found when the polarization of the photon generated by the first (second) decay is parallel to that of the first (second) pump beam. In contrast, the model consistently underestimates the experimental coincidence rates for the opposite polarization configuration. These findings indicate that effects beyond the internal level dynamics of individual atoms, most notably collective phenomena, are required to fully account for photon coincidences generated by four-wave mixing in atomic ensembles.
summary: This paper rigorously tests the single-atom model for four-wave mixing in cold atomic ensembles using polarization-resolved photon detection. The authors find excellent agreement for single-photon counts but observe systematic underestimation of coincidence rates for certain polarization channels. This discrepancy strongly suggests that collective atomic interactions, beyond individual level dynamics, are required for a complete theoretical description of the quantum light statistics.
main_problem: The study experimentally tests the limits of the single-atom model used to describe photon-pair generation via four-wave mixing (FWM) in cold atomic ensembles.
main_result: While the single-atom model accurately predicts single-photon counts, it consistently underestimates the measured coincidence rates for certain polarization configurations, suggesting that collective phenomena are necessary for a full description.
method: The authors developed a comprehensive, high-level single-atom model incorporating all relevant hyperfine and Zeeman sublevels, solving the dynamics using the Lindblad master equation, and comparing predictions to polarization-resolved experimental measurements.
model_or_system: The system uses a cold-atom source (e.g., Rb in a MOT) undergoing FWM in a diamond configuration. The model is a detailed 32-level description solved via the Lindblad master equation, accounting for complex internal atomic structure.
key_observables: Single-photon counts, coincidence rates ($G^{(2)}$) for various polarization channels (e.g., $G^{(2)}_{HV}$), and population dynamics of Zeeman sublevels.
important_parameters: Pump laser powers, detunings ($\delta_1, \delta_2$), and the inclusion/exclusion of a re-pump laser field.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation/assumption tested is the validity of the single-atom approximation; the discrepancy points to the necessity of including collective effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the minimal diamond FWM configuration and the full 32-level atomic system for Rb, while other figures compare calculated photon counts and coincidence rates against experimental data across varying laser powers.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem (FWM in atoms), details the advanced 32-level theoretical model (Hamiltonian, Lindblad equation), presents the experimental measurements (counts and coincidences), and concludes by comparing theory to experiment to identify the breakdown point of the single-atom approximation.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of open quantum systems modeling in AMO physics, specifically addressing when simple single-particle descriptions fail and when collective, many-body interactions (like dipole-dipole coupling) must be incorporated.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Minimal illustration of the diamond configuration for four-wave mixing. The cyclic process begins with the two-step excitation |1⟩→|2⟩→|3⟩, driven by two laser beams with Rabi frequencies Ω1 and Ω2 and corresponding detunings δ1 and δ2, respectively. Signal and idler photons are generated through the cascade decay |3⟩→|2⟩→|1⟩, with decay rates Γ1 and Γ2. The transition colors indicate orthogonal polarizations. The state |0⟩represents the lower hyperfine level of the alkali-atom ground state.

FIG. 2. Illustration of the complete atomic system considered in the model,IOP corresponding to a diamond configuration of transitions in 87Rb. (a) Relevant hyperfine levels, showing the two pump fields that drive the excitation transitions and the two spontaneous decay transitions, labeled by their corresponding wavelengths. (b) All mF projections included in the model. For clarity, only a representative subset of the excitation and decay transitions allowed by the corresponding selection rules is shown.

FIG. 3. Populations of all possible mF projections as a function of time. Panels (a)–(d) show the populations of the mF projections of the 5S1/2 F = 2, 5P3/2 F = 3, 5D3/2 F = 3, and 5P1/2 F = 2 levels without the re-pump laser. Panels (e)- (h) show the corresponding populations when the re-pump laser is included. Panels (i) and (j) show the populations of the auxiliary levels 5S1/2 F = 1 and 5P3/2 F = 2, which participate in the re-pump process. Results obtained via simulation with the MulAtoLEG Mathematica package.

FIG. 4. Schematic of the experimental apparatus. Pump 1 and pump 2 (left) are delivered to the main experiment through optical fibers and stabilized using two saturated-absorption spectroscopy setups. Their polarizations are prepared to be linear and orthogonal, and the beams are overlapped at interference filter IF1 so that they co-propagate through the center of the magneto-optical trap. A combined beam containing four wavelengths exits the vacuum chamber on the opposite side. Interference filter IF3 transmits only the signal photons, which are directed to the first quantum-tomography station equipped with APD1 and APD3. The theoretical calculations are based on the 32-level model.
